Although recent studies have revealed that CLas-associated reproductive enhancement involves neuroendocrine and neurotransmitter pathways, the transcriptional regulators linking persistent bacterial infection, energy metabolism, juvenile hormone (JH) signaling, and ovarian development remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the forkhead transcription factor DcFoxO as a previously unrecognized regulatory node associated with CLas-induced fecundity enhancement in D. citri. DcFoxO expression was significantly elevated in the ovaries of CLas-positive females during reproductive maturation. RNA interference-mediated silencing of DcFoxO reduced triacylglycerol and glycogen reserves, decreased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired ovarian development, reduced fecundity, and lowered CLas titers in the ovaries. Using dual-luciferase reporter assays, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), and microRNA (miRNA) gain-of-function experiments, we demonstrated that miR-176 directly targets the 3' untranslated region of DcFoxO and negatively regulates its expression. Overexpression of miR-176 phenocopied DcFoxO knockdown, suppressing energy reserves, ovarian development, fecundity, and CLas proliferation. Mechanistically, DcFoxO silencing or miR-176 overexpression reduced JH titers and down-regulated core JH-responsive reproductive genes, including DcMet, DcKr-h1, DcVg, and DcVgR. These findings reveal a miR-176-DcFoxO-JH regulatory axis that links CLas infection to metabolic reprogramming, ovarian maturation, and enhanced vector fecundity. This study adds a transcriptional layer to the emerging model of CLas-mediated manipulation of D. citri reproduction and identifies potential molecular targets for disrupting vector performance and HLB transmission. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: Anatomically Defined Motor Phenotypes Reveal Dissociated Trajectories of Progression, Neurofilament Profiles, and Survival in ALS.
abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) may reflect structured disease trajectories. This study investigated whether anatomically defined motor phenotypes capture reproducible patterns associated with progression, serum neurofilament light chain (NfL), and survival. In a multicenter cohort of 1307 ALS patients, motor phenotypes were classified by region of onset, timing of propagation to a vertically distant body region (early ≤ 12 months vs. later), and the degree of upper (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) dysfunction. Intercenter consistency was assessed using the Friedman test and Kendall's W. Associations with ALS progression rate (ALSPR), NfL, and survival were analyzed using group comparisons and Cox regression models. Phenotype classification was consistent across centers (Kendall's W 0.75-0.89). Onset phenotypes were significantly associated with ALSPR, NfL, and survival (p < 0.001). Trunk onset showed the lowest log(NfL/ALSPR), indicating dissociation between rapid progression and relative NfL elevation. Early propagation was the strongest marker of disease aggressiveness, with higher ALSPR, elevated NfL, and reduced survival (HR 2.93, p < 0.001). In early propagation, NfL disproportionally increased with progression indicating a relative uncoupling of NfL from functional decline. Phenotypes with balanced UMN/LMN and predominant LMN involvement were associated with shorter survival (HR 2.51, p < 0.001). Anatomically defined motor phenotypes identify reproducible ALS trajectories with distinct clinical and neurofilament profiles. Early propagation provides an actionable risk marker of disease aggressiveness, while combined upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction or lower motor neuron predominance is prognostically unfavorable. These findings support integrating structured phenotyping into prognostic models and clinical trial stratification.

title: Can kindness escape cruelty? Risks and benefits of incorporating kindness into regulatory culture.
abstract: Intelligent kindness has been proposed as a management model for reviving the UK welfare state and returning it to adequate functionality. Its goal, to deliver kindness as a core good, resembles that of the Liverpool Care Pathway (LCP), which sought to provide the compassion of hospice care across all end-of-life care, irrespective of setting. Analysis of the LCP's eventual failure suggests intelligent kindness faces similar risks, which can be avoided. Distinguishing between providing and enabling kindness, managing the relationship between kindness, material and cognitive resources, having dedicated staff to champion it past the roll-out stage, concurrent research planning and implementation, and careful management of its scope and boundaries as it becomes more mainstream should protect it, and help it become established as part of UK welfare regulatory culture.

title: CSF and plasma lipid profiling predicts risk of cognitive impairment in cognitively unimpaired older adults.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Age-related cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD) are strongly influenced by lipid metabolism, yet how central and peripheral lipid profiles relate to disease risk before symptom onset remains unclear. We performed comprehensive shotgun lipidomics in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma from cognitively unimpaired older adults, with longitudinal follow-up for Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) conversion. CSF lipidomes were primarily associated with age and established CSF AD biomarkers, whereas plasma lipid profiles were strongly influenced by sex. Specific CSF phosphatidylethanolamine subspecies showed robust positive associations with CSF total tau, phosphorylated tau 181, neurogranin, and chitinase-3 like-1. CSF triacylglycerol TAG(C49:6), phosphatidylglycerol PG(18:0-18:1), cholesteryl ester CE(20:3), and phosphatidylethanolamine PE(D16:0-18:1) independently predicted CDR conversion, improving risk prediction. Plasma sphingomyelin subspecies were modestly associated with cognitive decline risk. These findings identify distinct CSF and plasma lipid signatures linked to preclinical cognitive decline and highlight brain lipid metabolism as a promising source of predictive biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Intracisternal injection of two human SOD1 aggregate strains induces templated aggregation and ALS in transgenic mouse model.
abstract: Cytosolic aggregates containing misfolded superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) protein is an established hallmark of ALS caused by mutations in the SOD1 gene. We have previously identified two structurally distinct strains of human (h) SOD1 aggregates (denoted A and B) in mice transgenic (Tg) for hSOD1. Strain A and B have both been shown to transmit templated aggregation and induce early-onset of fatal ALS-like disease when injected directly into the spinal cord or peripheral nerve of hSOD1 Tg mice. In contrast, peripheral administration of hSOD1 aggregates into the intraperitoneal cavity or skeletal muscle did not induce disease. Collectively, these studies provide insight on the spreading mechanism of SOD1. However, the complete map of propagation routes and underlying mechanisms utilized by SOD1 aggregates in ALS is not fully charted. Here, we investigated whether hSOD1 aggregates may spread to the central nervous system (CNS) via the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Mutant hSOD1 aggregate seeds or control samples prepared from spinal cords of hSOD1 Tg mice or non-Tg mice, respectively, were inoculated into the cisterna magna of adult 100-day-old Tg mice expressing the G85R mutated hSOD1 protein. Disease phenotyping as well as biochemical and immunohistochemical analyses were performed and compared across the experimental groups. The mice inoculated with hSOD1 seeds developed early signs of ALS by 90 days after inoculation and reached terminal stage approximately 180 days earlier than mice receiving control seeds. Additionally, both strain A and B were observed to initiate templated aggregation along the neuroaxis. The results show that hSOD1 aggregates are capable of transmitting from the CSF to the CNS where they induce ALS-like pathology and concomitant phenotype. Unraveling the propagation pathways utilized by SOD1 opens new avenues to assess treatment strategies against ALS.

title: Cost-effectiveness of lecanemab for early Alzheimer's disease in China.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Although lecanemab has demonstrated clinical efficacy in early Alzheimer's disease (AD), its cost-effectiveness in China remains uncertain. This study evaluated the long-term cost-effectiveness of lecanemab in Chinese patients from a societal perspective and estimated its value-based price (VBP). A Markov state transition model based on Chinese real-world data was developed to compare the long-term health progression and economic outcomes of lecanemab combined with standard of care (SoC) versus SoC alone. Compared to SoC alone, the lecanemab combination therapy gained an additional 1.2432 Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) at an incremental cost of 463,228 Chinese yuan (CNY), resulting in an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of 372,609 CNY/QALY (≈ 52,783 USD/QALY). To achieve cost-effectiveness within the willingness-to-pay threshold, the price of a single vial of lecanemab must be reduced by at least 18.0%. Lecanemab can provide health benefits to Chinese patients with early AD, but it is not cost-effective under the current pricing system.

title: Neurocognitive training with visual perturbation improves dual-task hop performance in male athletes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Returning to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) carries high re-injury risk and persistent functional impairments. Sensorimotor control changes not addressed by standard rehabilitation may lead to neurological compensations affecting functional performance and psychological readiness. Specifically, neural activity associated with sensory, visual, and cognitive processing is elevated for knee motor control in ACLR patients compared to healthy controls. Therefore, developing complementary therapies that target injury-related neuroplasticity may improve rehabilitation effectiveness in resolving both functional and psychological deficits. Twenty-four athletes post-ACLR randomized into Visual-Cognitive Neuromuscular Training (VCNT, n = 12) or Visual-Cognitive Neuromuscular Training with stroboscopic glasses (VCNT-S, n = 12). Both groups trained 3x/week for 8 weeks with neuromuscular exercises combined with cognitive dual-tasks. X-hop performance and Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK) assessed pre- and post-intervention. Both groups improved functional performance from pretest to post test. For the ACLR limb, the VCNT group improved from 349.78 ± 8.62 to 367.57 ± 5.35 (5.08% change), while the VCNT-S group improved from 347.44 ± 8.14 to 375.48 ± 5.1 (8.07% change). For the uninvolved limb, the VCNT group improved from 355 ± 6.79 to 370.09 ± 5.57 (4.25% change), while the VCNT-S group improved from 352.35 ± 6.86 to 378.59 ± 4.65 (7.45% change). The group * time interaction was significant for both limbs, favoring VCNT-S over VCNT (ACLR limb: interaction effect size = 1.00, p-interaction = 0.01; uninvolved limb: interaction effect size = 1.19; p-interaction = 0.01) Regarding fear of movement, both group showed improvement (VCNT: 4.25 ± 2.73, % change = -18.09%; VCNT-S group: 4.66 ± 3.67, % change = -19.66%) relative to their pre-test scores, but no significant differences were found between the groups (P-Interaction = 0.4, interaction effect size = 0.29). In addition, hop improvements for both limbs showed weak, non-significant correlations with kinesiophobia reduction (ACLR: r = 0.08, p = 0.71; uninvolved: r = 0.17, p = 0.43). VCNT-S improved hop performance under dual-task conditions beyond VCNT alone. Adding visual perturbation to VCNT may be able to further improve functional performance and readiness for return to sport. However, psychological readiness may not uniquely benefit from stroboscopic training but does benefit from VCNT generally. Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT), IRCT20250314065070N1. Date of Registration: 3 June 2025, retrospective registration.

title: Diagnostic evaluation of long-read nanopore sequencing for pediatric CNS tumors.
abstract: Long-read nanopore sequencing enables methylation-based CNS tumor classification while providing additional genomic information within a single assay. However, its performance across molecular features relevant to pediatric CNS tumor diagnostics and across available methylation classifiers remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated nanopore sequencing for integrated molecular characterization of pediatric CNS tumors and compared with data from DNA methylation arrays and Illumina short-read sequencing used in the clinical diagnostic work-up. Twenty tumor samples representing three major pediatric CNS tumor groups (gliomas, ependymomas and medulloblastomas) were subjected to long-read nanopore sequencing, which generated robust long-read data across all tumor groups, with a mean genome coverage of approximately 40x. Nanopore-derived copy-number profiles showed good concordance with methylation array-derived profiles (median Pearson r = 0.816). Nanopore evidence was identified for 74/78 (95%) clinically relevant small variants detected by Illumina sequencing, although 53/78 (68%) were recovered as exact high-confidence nanopore calls. Structural variant profiles showed limited breakpoint overlap and differed in the number, type, and size distribution of detected events between Illumina and Nanopore sequencing. Nanopore-derived methylation classifications were largely concordant with integrated WHO CNS5 diagnoses. Ependymomas, medulloblastomas, and pilocytic astrocytomas, were concordantly classified across all evaluated classifiers, although not all classifications reached the respective classifier-specific confidence thresholds. In contrast, diffuse gliomas showed greater variability in classification across classifiers. Downsampling indicated that concordance with integrated WHO CNS5 diagnoses remained high at substantially reduced sequencing depths, whereas the proportion of classifications reaching classifier-specific confidence thresholds was more classifier dependent. Long-read nanopore sequencing enables integrated molecular characterization of pediatric CNS tumors within a single assay, although concordance with established methods varied by genomic feature and tumor type. The preservation of methylation classification performance at reduced sequencing depth supports the feasibility of shorter sequencing workflows. Prospective studies are required to establish performance and turnaround time in routine clinical diagnostics.

title: Plasma β-synuclein associates with hippocampal synaptic density measured with [11C]UCB-J PET and plasma tau markers in Alzheimer's disease.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Plasma β-synuclein is a promising blood-based synaptic biomarker, but relationships with synaptic density as indicated by [11C]UCB-J positron emission tomography (PET), and blood biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology, neurodegeneration, and astrocyte activation need further characterization. Middle-aged and older adults with and without cognitive impairment (N = 83 total, 68.7% cognitively unimpaired) underwent blood draw, PET imaging, and neuropsychological testing. Primary analyses focused on relationships between plasma β-synuclein and synaptic density, and associations with related plasma biomarkers (tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 [p-tau217], brain-derived tau [BD-tau], glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP], and neurofilament light chain [NfL]). Plasma β-synuclein levels were higher in cognitively unimpaired and impaired participants with positive amyloid PET. Synaptic density was lower in cognitively impaired participants only. In the full sample, higher plasma β-synuclein levels associated with lower synaptic density in the hippocampus, higher concentrations of plasma tau markers, and higher plasma GFAP. This work further supports utilization of plasma β-synuclein to track synaptic degeneration in AD.

title: PROMISE: a PROspective randomised double-blind parallel group placebo-controlled multicentre trial of faecal MIcrobiota tranSplantation to improve outcomEs in patients with cirrhosis over 24 months-study protocol for a clinical trial.
abstract: Patients with cirrhosis have reduced gut bacterial diversity and a gut microbiota dominated by pathobionts. These changes, coupled with increased gut permeability and bacterial translocation, increase susceptibility to infection and death. There is also considerable concern that high antimicrobial exposure in the cirrhotic population drives the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We previously performed a randomised feasibility trial of endoscopically administered jejunal faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) slurry derived from stringently screened donors, and showed it to be safe and well-tolerated in patients with cirrhosis (PROFIT Trial: NCT02862249). FMT was associated with reduced enteropathogenic bacteria in the gut, augmented ammonia excretion, ameliorated systemic inflammation, and enhanced innate immune responses to pathogen challenge. The trial was not powered to detect differences in clinical outcomes. The PROMISE study will evaluate the efficacy of lyophilised encapsulated FMT to reduce infection, decompensating events and mortality in patients with cirrhosis secondary to alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) cirrhosis and metabolic dysfunction and alcohol-related liver disease (MetALD). The PROMISE study is a phase 3 multicentre, randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial that will evaluate encapsulated lyophilised FMT in 300 participants with ALD, MetALD or MASLD cirrhosis (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease Sodium (MELD-Na) score 8-16). Participants will be randomly allocated (1:1) to receive FMT or matched placebo capsules every 91 days for 21 months, with 24-month follow-up. The primary endpoint is time-to-infection or decompensating event resulting in presentation to the emergency department or hospitalisation. Secondary endpoints include all hepatic decompensation, all-cause infection, antibiotic usage, incidence of AMR, hospitalisation rates, liver disease severity scores, quality of life scores, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale score (HADS), alcohol use, and mortality. Mechanistic endpoints include quantification of plasma bacterial DNA, plasma and faecal cytokines/biomarkers, plasma and faecal metabolome, faecal proteome, faecal microbiome composition and diversity (including resistome) and monocyte and mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell frequency, phenotype and function. Recruitment commenced in June 2023. Results will be disseminated via peer-reviewed journals, international conferences and patient support groups. The PROMISE study will assess the efficacy and evaluate the mechanisms of action of FMT in patients with ALD, MASLD and MetALD cirrhosis. FMT may provide an alternative non-antibiotic treatment for these patients through ecological reconstitution of microbial balance. ISRCTN, ISRCTN17863382. title: Discordance between pupillometry indices: a matter of scale and sedation.
Adult ADHD, PARK2 copy number variations and the blood-brain barrier: Culture duration-dependent metabolic alterations in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived in vitro models.
journal: Fluids and barriers of the CNS
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a multifactorial neurodevelopmental disorder in which PARK2 copy number variations (CNVs) constitute a rare genetic risk factor. PARK2 encodes parkin, a key regulator of mitochondrial quality control. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in ADHD pathophysiology and can contribute to blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. As BBB disruption remains insufficiently understood in ADHD, this study investigated whether adult ADHD and PARK2 CNVs are accompanied by alterations in BBB phenotype, mitochondrial properties, and cellular metabolism. Brain capillary endothelial-like cells (BCECs) were generated using 10 donor-specific human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines from adults with ADHD carrying PARK2 CNVs, alongside PARK2 wild type adults with and without ADHD. BCECs were analyzed at the end of differentiation (day 10) and after prolonged culture (day 17) to assess group-associated phenotypes and culture duration-dependent differences. Across all groups, BCECs showed brain endothelial marker expression, high transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER), and low sodium fluorescein (NaFl) permeability at day 10. After prolonged culture, NaFl permeability remained low, whereas TEER-based barrier integrity declined. Prolonged culture of BCECs reduced glycolytic ATP production rates while increasing mitochondrial ATP production and its relative contribution to total ATP production, reflecting a metabolic shift from glycolysis toward oxidative phosphorylation. Despite decreased total ATP production after prolonged culture, cellular energy status was largely preserved, alongside overall lower intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitochondrial membrane potential. At day 10, BCECs from ADHD donors carrying PARK2 duplications displayed greater mitochondrial abundance, the highest basal and oxidative stress-induced intracellular ROS levels, and reduced TEER-based barrier integrity, while at day 17, BCECs from ADHD donors with PARK2 deletions exhibited the least glycolysis-dependent ATP production profile, although absolute mitochondrial ATP production remained comparable between groups. Prolonged culture was associated with broad, ADHD- and PARK2 genotype-independent metabolic remodeling, whereas mitochondrial and metabolic alterations associated with ADHD and PARK2 CNVs were overall small. This study identifies culture duration as a critical parameter for the characterization of hiPSC-derived BBB in vitro models and supports the feasibility of using donor-specific BCECs at the end of differentiation to investigate BBB-associated mechanisms in adult ADHD and PARK2 CNVs.

title: Short-interval variability and test-retest reliability of Alzheimer's disease plasma biomarkers in a clinically heterogenous cohort.
abstract: Assessment of short-term within-subject variability and test-retest reliability of Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related plasma biomarkers is important for real-world clinical implementation and interpretation in research studies. In this study we aimed to assess short-term variability and reliability of core AD plasma biomarkers, proposed ratios, and evaluate a broader proteomic panel. Two serial plasma samples were collected from each of the 92 participants enrolled in observational research studies over intervals ranging from 30 minutes to three months. Test-retest reliability and within-subject variability were assessed for 131 biomarkers measured on three immunoassays (Lumipulse G plasma p-tau217; Fujirebio, NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel and NULISAqpcr AD 5-Plex; Alamar Biosciences). We subsequently evaluated the stability of a dual cut-point approach for AD probability diagnostic categorisation and examined whether within-subject variability was associated with inter-sample interval (time between serial blood sampling). All core AD plasma biomarkers assessed in this study (Aβ42, BD-p-tau181, BD-p-tau217, BD-p-tau231, p-tau181, p-tau217, p-tau231, GFAP and NfL) demonstrated strong correlations (r ≥ 0.79) and high reliability (ICC ≥ 0.84). Within-subject variability was moderate to low for core AD plasma biomarkers. Using a validated dual cut-point approach for plasma p-tau217, most individuals (92%) remained within the same diagnostic category (high/indeterminate/low) across both timepoints, and no individual moved across two boundaries (i.e. from high to low AD probability categorisation or vice versa). For the majority of analytes, within-subject variability was not associated with inter-sample interval after adjustment for age and sex, however, the core AD plasma biomarker, NfL did have a significant association. While core AD plasma biomarkers had limited variability and high reliability over short-intervals, other central nervous system (CNS)-relevant biomarkers showed greater variability, which may be relevant for interpretation in association studies and clinical applications.

title: BTBD9-driven IMPDH2 ubiquitination governs sleep homeostasis by gating adenosine metabolism in the basal forebrain.
abstract: BTB domain containing 9 (BTBD9) is among the most reproducible genetic risk factors for sleep-related disorders, yet its molecular function in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we aimed to define the downstream substrate, core brain region, and molecular mechanism through which BTBD9 regulates sleep-wake homeostasis. Population-scale genomic and brain expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) datasets were integrated to infer the direction of BTBD9-associated genetic risk in sleep-related traits. Basal forebrain-specific neuronal manipulation of Btbd9 was combined with electroencephalography/electromyography (EEG/EMG)-based sleep analysis and fiberphotomerty to define the relevant brain locus and functional output. Ubiquitinomics, protein interaction, ubiquitination, and enzymatic assays were used to identify BTBD9-regulated substrates and determine how BTBD9-dependent modification affects metabolic enzyme activity. Basal forebrain-specific genetic disruption, receptor pharmacology, and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered interfering peptides were further applied to test pathway necessity and reversibility in vivo. human genetic analyses showed that BTBD9 variants associated with higher expression predicted a pro-arousal tendency. Consistently, neuron-specific deletion of Btbd9 in the mouse basal forebrain increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and extracellular adenosine levels. Mechanistically, IMPDH2, the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine biosynthesis, was identified as a substrate of the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 (CRL3)BTBD9 ubiquitin ligase. BTBD9-mediated ubiquitination at IMPDH2 lysine 195 (K195) relieved guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-dependent allosteric inhibition, thereby limiting adenosine accumulation and sleep pressure. Basal forebrain neuronal knockout of Impdh2 recapitulated the sleep-promoting effect of Btbd9 deletion, whereas adenosine A1 receptor (A1R) blockade attenuated this phenotype. AAV-delivered interfering peptides targeting the BTBD9-IMPDH2 interaction reduced IMPDH2 ubiquitination, elevated adenosine levels, increased NREM sleep, and rescued BTBD9 overexpression-induced abnormal wakefulness in vivo. These findings identify a BTBD9-IMPDH2-adenosine pathway that links human genetic risk to basal forebrain control of sleep homeostasis. By defining BTBD9 as a molecular regulator of purine metabolism, this study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding and potentially targeting BTBD9-related sleep dysregulation.

title: Hormone replacement therapy through the lens of epigenetic clock: estrogen signals, glycemic status, and lifespan.
abstract: Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) is a critical biomarker of aging. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is commonly used to alleviate age-related diseases, while glycemic status also influences the aging process. We aimed to investigate the association between estrogen and EAA, and the effects of HRT, EAA, and glycemic status on mortality. Mendelian randomization (MR) established causal relationships between genetically predicted estrogen receptor expression and EAA markers (HorvathAA, HannumAA, PhenoAA, and GrimAA). Using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, we employed Cox proportional hazards models to analyze the association between HRT and mortality, exploring whether it was modified by EAA and glycemic status. Elevated estrogen receptor α (ESR1) expression significantly decelerated PhenoAA (β -1.26; 95% CI: -2.16, -0.37; P = 0.005). HRT significantly correlated with a reduced risk of all-cause (HR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.47-0.88; P = 0.006) and cardiovascular (HR: 0.52, 95% CI: 0.28-0.95; P = 0.033) mortality. Additionally, there was a significant three-way interaction among HRT, two types of EAA (HorvathAA and PhenoAA), and abnormal glucose status. Stratified analyses showed no significant interaction in the normal glucose subgroup; however, a significant antagonistic interaction emerged between HRT and both HorvathAA and PhenoAA in the abnormal glucose subgroup. Consequently, although HRT exhibited a protective main effect in patients with abnormal glucose, its survival benefits were significantly attenuated as their epigenetic aging accelerated. Estrogen may decelerate PhenoAA via the ESR1 pathway. In postmenopausal women, HRT is significantly associated with a reduced risk of mortality; however, this survival benefit is substantially modified by glycemic status. Future studies should evaluate whether incorporating EAA and glycemic status into HRT decision-making could optimize clinical outcomes.
